    #21899. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1694 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
    • According to recent reports, gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
    • The journey has not gone according to plan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

    According to recent reports, gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

    The journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

    It has been revealed that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

    How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

    Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid looks. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

    Recent findings suggest that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

    How much has the weather affected your progress?

    Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

    For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

    Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

    Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

    By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

    Recent findings suggest that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

    What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

    It has been revealed that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

    I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

    Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

    It has been revealed that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

    The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

    What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

    Recent findings suggest that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

    Recent findings suggest that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

    Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

    Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

    The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

    I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

    Industry observers note that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

    Sources indicate that we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

    There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

    How did you first get into the sport?

    Sources indicate that I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

    Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

    Industry observers note that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

    Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

    The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

    Industry observers note that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

    It has been revealed that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

    You can follow the expedition here.

    #21894. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (388 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
    • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
    • It has been revealed that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is rapidly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

    “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

    It has been revealed that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

    It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

    According to recent reports, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

    On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

    Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

    #21890. Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (341 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (341 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
    • Industry observers note that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
    • The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

    Industry observers note that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

    The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

    Recent findings suggest that eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

    It has been revealed that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He noted climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

    The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

    The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

    Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

    Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

    Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

    This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

    With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

    Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
    • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
    • Industry observers note that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

    The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

    Industry observers note that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

    “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

    According to recent reports, this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

    “The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

    The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

    Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

    Recent findings suggest that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse.
    • I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water.
    • It has been revealed that at 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse. After days of walking against the main flow of pilgrims, yesterday was the first time we had the trail mostly to ourselves—aside from the crowds packing onto the upriver boats.

    I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water. Watching the sun light up the morning sky with a plate of boiled quail eggs and a couple of strong cups of espresso was a wonderfully peaceful start. Today was billed as one of the most scenic and spiritual sections of the entire Camino.

    It has been revealed that at 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water. The sun was just over the horizon, casting warm rays across the long footbridge as we crossed a small inlet bay to hike along the coast.

    Sources indicate that after walking along the coast for a bit, the trail angled inland. Following a slight climb up to a small church, we made our first wrong turn of the day.

    Once we realized we were off the official Camino, we decided to forge our own path using Google Maps rather than backtrack.

    Industry observers note that the route crossed a high bridge over a busy highway before diving into a peaceful forest. Climbing up, we looked back and were amazed to see how far away the coast already looked. We could see the bay, distant coastal cities, and mountains on the horizon—all after just an hour and a half of walking.

    Sources indicate that as we exited the trees, we stumbled upon a massive vineyard stretching out across the hills. Unfortunately, the winery wasn’t open for another 20 minutes, so we kept moving. Walking through endless fields of grapes was incredible, and skipping the wine stop turned out to be a blessing given what the trail had in store for us later.

    Walking against the grain of the Camino created endless confusion for everyone we passed:.

    Sources indicate that they became genuinely concerned for us, which we thought was endearing. Every time we ran into a local, we used a mix of butchered Spanish and sign language to explain we were hiking toward Porto. Other times, we just smiled, waved, and kept moving.

    We were deep in the countryside, passing beautiful solid-stone homes with immaculate gardens and tiny backyard vineyards.

    By mid-morning, we had already knocked out 9 miles in under three hours.

    Industry observers note that we spotted the only café we’d seen all morning, grabbed a coffee and black tea, and relaxed on the porch overlooking the river. With such a fast pace early on, we assumed the rest of the day would be a breeze. We were very wrong.

    The path ran right alongside the river for the next mile. The water was teeming with huge, two-foot-long fish—an invasive species, I assumed, since the river was practically overflowing with them. As the shade disappeared, the heat began to rise quickly.

    In a recent development, at the junction of two busy multilane highways, we tried crossing via an elevated pedestrian bridge. As we climbed, thick briers started crowding the walkway—a red flag I should have noticed sooner. Reaching the other side, I realized we were totally off-track. We backtracked over the highway and ended up at a massive roundabout packed with nonstop traffic. Fortunately, we spotted a pedestrian tunnel to get us safely across.

    In a recent development, on the other side of the highway, we stopped at a small roadside restaurant. This was a crucial stop: there were no grocery stores, cafés, or towns along our next stretch of the route.

    We ordered the local Pilgrim’s Menu:.

    Before leaving, I refilled our water bottles from the bathroom sink, knowing we were heading into a dry, rural stretch.

    The next 5.5 km section was advertised as a tranquil forest trail running along a bubbling river with numerous waterfalls, climbing gently up to the Mosteiro de Santa María da Armenteira.

    Since we couldn’t get a room at the monastery, our blueprint was to split off the Camino early and head to our accommodation in the tiny village of Silva. Armed with Google Maps, I figured it would be an easy shortcut.

    Hot, tired, and out of water, we took a brief breather in a shaded cove when a cool breeze finally offered a moment of relief.

    After climbing along the creek for 5 km, we left the Camino to forge our own path to Silva.

    Industry observers note that what started as a narrow, paved road rapidly turned into a steep, unpaved logging trail climbing straight up through the forest. On Google Maps, it looked like a legitimate road; in reality, it was an overgrown, barely used dirt track.

    I started to question: were we climbing all this way just to hit a dead end and be forced to hike all the way back down?

    It has been revealed that knockerz was melting, I was completely exhausted, and we were both soaked in sweat and desperately thirsty. I hit that dazed, survival-mode state where you just keep putting one foot in front of the other, hoping the hill ends soon.

    We kept pushing up the incline until, suddenly, the dirt track broke through the trees and met a paved road leading right to our door. Google Maps had come through.

    Our lodging was a small, unmanned albergue with eight rooms and a shared kitchen.

    In a recent development, upon arrival our first stop was to hydrate. We went straight into the shared kitchen and drank glass after glass of cold water.

    Sources indicate that next stop was to shower. We each took showers with our clothes on to rinse the caked-on sweat and dirt off both our bodies and gear at the same time.

    Laying in the bed we were glad this day was done.

    #21873. Tech Report: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (600 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
    • Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
    • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

    Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

    Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

    “My initiative is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he remarked.

    According to recent reports, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

    Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

    Industry observers note that lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

    The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

    According to recent reports, kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

    Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line presently being attempted by a Russian team.

    This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

    It has been revealed that kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

    Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

    #21869. Industry News: What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (801 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people.
    • In a recent development, but getting to the trail takes more than a dream.
    • Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people. Spanning 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada, the trail offers the opportunity to step away from everyday life, immerse yourself in the outdoors, and experience something that can be difficult to put into words.

    In a recent development, but getting to the trail takes more than a dream. For many aspiring thru-hikers, the financial commitment is one of the biggest barriers. Between gear, food, transportation, and the ability to step away from work for several months, the cost of a thru-hike can put the experience out of reach before someone even takes their first step.

    The PCT Grant was created to help change that.

    Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. Its mission is to make long-distance hiking more accessible by easing the financial burden and giving someone the opportunity to pursue an experience they might not otherwise be able to afford.

    At its heart, the program is about expanding access to the outdoors and recognizing that the transformative experiences found on trail shouldn’t be limited to those who can afford them.

    2026 was the first year the PCT Grant came to life and chose its first recipient to take on thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. That person was me! The face behind the screen: Cappy. Post trail, I have joined the PCT Grant Committee to spread some magic with hopes of creating that same opportunity for others.

    According to recent reports, receiving the grant was a lifeline. It wasn’t just financial support; it was the difference between being able to pursue this dream and having to put it on hold. It gave me room to take a chance on myself and say yes to an experience that changed the way I see what’s possible in life.

    As this year’s recipient, I experienced firsthand what this kind of support can make possible. The trail taught me a lot about the power of choice and trust. The power of choosing something before knowing exactly how it will unfold, doing it scared, and learning to become comfortable with the uncomfortable.

    According to recent reports, spending five months on trail offered so much more than the physical accomplishment of a thru-hike. I discovered how much we are capable of when we give ourselves the opportunity to find out. This trail changed my life, and it will continue to do so.

    As the program enters its second year, the focus is on growing awareness, strengthening community support, and building a foundation for future recipients.

    According to recent reports, currently, the grant is funded to support one hiker annually, with a longer-term vision of expanding its reach and helping more aspiring thru-hikers access the trail. From our fundraising efforts (a post trail Q&A with Cappy and other media platforms helping to spread the word) we have raised enough money to fund a second hiker this coming year.

    Donations play an notable role in making that possible. Every contribution helps sustain the program and move it closer to supporting additional hikers in the years ahead. We want to continue to grow this program so that even more hikers can set foot on the trail.

    Sources indicate that applications for the 2027 PCT Grant are open through January 31, 2027. If you’re a Washingtonian between 18 and 33 with a dream of hiking the PCT, this could be an opportunity to make it happen.

    And for those who have already experienced the magic of the trail, consider helping someone else get there.

    Help make the next journey possible.

    Learn more about the PCT Grant | Donate to the Trail Angel Fund.

    #21863. Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (932 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

    Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk.
    • Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.
    • Industry observers note that as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk. At least 9 hours, too, which was way more than I had been getting.

    Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.

    Industry observers note that as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew. The girl was my age, and we discussed the Camino ending and what our lives would be like once we returned home. She was studying to be an actress and wanted to do so for the passion of it and to help people, not for the money or to be famous. She held many side jobs as a way to pay for her education and dream, one of them being teaching theater to children in a church. She spoke of the importance of giving young people a spiritual outlet, in whatever way felt best to them.

    According to recent reports, the conversation then turned to my job and coaching. After telling her I help people find holistic balance in their life, she curiously asked me:.

    “How do you find balance in your life?”.

    Industry observers note that this started a beautiful conversation about how we each live our lives, the things we prioritize, and our outlook on happiness and peace. A girl I’d met only a few days prior suddenly felt so familiar.

    But then up ahead, I saw the brothers.

    In a recent development, I yelled to them, and they waited for me to approach. With hugs and excitement, we all decided to go to a local restaurant, A Garnacha, for traditional Galician pulpo (octopus).

    With three orders of pulpo in front of us, we dove into the tentacles with the toothpicks we were given as utensils. Not many words were remarked as we devoured our plates. The boys asked if I liked it, and the best I could say was,.

    “No es mi favorita, pero me gusta.”.

    For the first time in the whole Camino, the three of us walked together. Of course the Italian brother walked ahead, but we were still in close proximity.

    The three of us dropped our packs at a pilgrim rest area, and ended up spending over an hour there.

    We sang for the pilgrims that passed.

    We laughed while we rested all together.

    Sources indicate that my Argentinian brother and I were shocked by the fact that our Italian brother sat for that long. Having just bought his plane ticket home, he was feeling the weight of the Camino ending and wanted to slow down over the next few days.

    He compared it to the last piece of pizza, and how you want to savor every single bite.

    We were all savoring each moment together like it was the last piece of pizza.

    It has been revealed that the last part of the walk we did independently. I came up to a stream with a beautiful stone bridge over top. I took the moment to stop and be still, watching the ripples of the water reflect on the bridge. I pulled acorns out of the cold water and made a game of throwing them at a rock.

    Simplicity. That’s what I love about this lifestyle, and something I will greatly miss.

    When I arrived in the town of Arzúa and made it to the municipal albergue, Xunta de Galicia Arzúa Pilgrims Hostel, I showered and collapsed on my bunk.

    My Italian brother came and got me once our Argentinian brother arrived, and we all walked to a restaurant in search of Galician barbecue. They were out of the barbecue we were looking for, so we ordered almost the entire menu instead.

    Homemade croquettes, pimientos de Padrón (peppers), mixed salad, raxo, and milanesa de pollo.

    In a recent development, there was not a crumb left. We got cheesecake and flan to top it off while the boys talked about the intersection of futbol and politics. I completely zoned out and started to see just how tired we all were.

    That became quite evident in the street as we walked to find gelato. There was so much giggling and play, especially because we were delusional with exhaustion. But at one point, I walked behind the two of them as they were carrying on and thought,.

    “I love these two so damn much.”.

    And with a generous cone of gelato before bed, we all crashed for our last substantial day.

She fell in love with long walks in nature during her Appalachian Trail 2022 thruhike where she dove into finding herself through the space that the trail provided. Since completing her flip-flop at Springer Mountain, she has crafted her lifestyle to travel full-time and serve others within her passion of holistic health. This walk is another step into the unknown to embark on "A Saunter of Spirit" as she raises awareness for mental health through raising money for Hike For Mental Health.
